title: Field Pocket Reference — Inference Tradeoffs & Opposition Maps
author: Leah Park
body:
Summary

This pocket reference is intended for field engineers, solution architects, and account teams to rapidly prepare for technical buyer conversations and competitive pushback. It consolidates concise positioning, buyer-specific messaging, a one-page competitive snapshot, priced scenario examples, a short customer case vignette, and a focused Security FAQ for prospects. Use this during discovery, technical calls, and pricing negotiations when differentiation needs to be precise and operationally grounded.

Target audience

- Solution architects and sales engineers
- Platform engineering leads evaluating inference economics
- Procurement/security stakeholders during RFP/pre-contract reviews

Positioning pillars (elevator + proof points)

1) Production-first economics: predictable latency and per-token unit costs.
   - Proof: Dedicated capacity and autoscale that preserve latency SLOs; intelligent batching reduces per-token cost by up to 3x for median request patterns.
2) Unified runtime across environments: same API/operational model for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.
   - Proof: Model pinning + rollout policies and identical observability tooling (Console) across deployment modes.
3) Fail-safe reliability and graceful degradation.
   - Proof: Smart routing, automatic fallback to model variants, and cross-region routing to maintain availability under capacity pressure.

Messaging by buyer persona (short scripts)

- Platform engineer (interests: observability, SLOs, cost):
  "Redwood gives your team a single control plane for inference so you can treat the model endpoint like any other internal service. You get token-level cost and latency breakdowns, tracing hooks, and policies to route by cost or latency—so predictable SLOs and budgeting become operational rather than guesswork."

- ML engineer (interests: model quality, rollout):
  "We support model variants, automatic fallback, and can run canary rollouts with sample-matched traffic. Our runtime preserves KV cache and lets you test quantized variants without code changes so you can validate quality + cost tradeoffs before rollouts."

- Security/compliance decision maker (interests: data residency, auditability):
  "Private deployments include a customer-managed control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logging. We can supply SOC2-scope evidence and network diagrams for architecture review—your security team keeps the keys and the logs."

Competitive snapshot (one-page)

Columns: Competitor | Strength | Primary Weakness vs Redwood | Battle tactic
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Major cloud AI endpoints | Broad managed infra, single-vendor convenience | Higher per-token cost for sustained throughput; limited built-in model fallback options | Lead with predictable economics and multi-deployment flexibility; show per-token TCO slides from customer scenario.
| Simpler LLM APIs | Easy dev UX and lower entry barrier | No dedicated capacity, fewer observability controls, limited SLAs | Emphasize SLOs, dedicated pools, and enterprise support for production workloads.
| Self-hosted runtime vendors | Deep customization, cost control at scale | Heavy ops burden and slower time-to-production; fragmented tooling | Position Redwood as managed + opinionated runtime that offloads ops while keeping cost controls.

Top competitive concerns and rebuttals

- "We can just self-host cheaper."
  - Rebuttal: Total cost of ownership includes engineering time, reliability engineering, and model runtime optimization. Redwood bundles optimized kernels, routing, and caching—reducing ongoing ops spend and time to recover from incidents. Use our TCO spreadsheet during pilots.
- "Vendor lock-in worries."
  - Rebuttal: API compatibility and model pinning make migration away incremental; we provide exportable configs and guidance, and private deployment options reduce lock-in risk.

Pricing guidance (concise scenarios)

Principles to state up-front:
- Hosted API is best for quick pilots and variable demand.
- Dedicated capacity is recommended when predictable throughput and latency are required.
- Private deployments incur platform fees and support contracts for on-prem/VPC.

Three short scenarios (use in field slides):

1) Pilot — conversational assistant (low volume): Hosted API using an open LLM; cost dominated by per-token spend. Est. monthly: $1.5k–$6k depending on traffic. Key ask: 90-day pilot credits + success metrics (latency <200ms P95, completion-error <2%).

2) Scale — consumer product (100K monthly active users): Dedicated pool; autoscaling with burst. Est. monthly: committed capacity $12k–$45k + per-token incremental. Key ask: 6–12 month reserve; SLA targets and costing windows.

3) Regulated enterprise — PII and residency: Private deployment (VPC) with KMS + audit logging. Est. first-year: onboarding and platform license $80k–$250k + infra ops. Key ask: security review, data processing addendum, on-site/remote onboarding timeline.

Negotiation levers for the field

- Trial credits and extended pilots in exchange for usage commitments.
- Predictable pricing tiers for committed qps; overage rates clearly defined.
- Professional services for model onboarding and quantization assistance as billable add-on or bundled in enterprise package.

Short case vignette (1-paragraph)

Customer: Fintech SMB — problem: slow model responses and runaway inference costs during peak trading hours. Outcome: Migrated to Redwood Dedicated with burst capacity and KV caching. Result: 2.8x reduction in median per-token compute cost during spikes, P95 latency improved from 1.2s to 220ms, and the customer avoided two critical incidents that previously required an emergency scale-up.

Security FAQ (field-ready answers)

Q: Where is customer data stored and who can access it?
A: Hosted: data persisted in region selected by the customer, access controlled via RBAC and audit logs. Dedicated/Private: customer controls storage/network; Redwood access governed by contract and emergency access policies.

Q: Do you support customer-managed keys?
A: Yes — KMS/HSM integrations available for Private and Dedicated where required.

Q: How do you demonstrate compliance posture?
A: We provide SOC2 Type II reports, pen test summaries, and can supply an architecture security appendix for enterprise reviews. Specific attestation artifacts are shared under NDA.

Q: What happens on a security incident?
A: Standard incident response with customer notification timelines, forensic evidence sharing, and post-incident remediation plans. For Private deployments, the customer lead owns the initial containment measures.

Pitch deck and assets (what to bring to the call)

- 5-slide technical appendix: runtime architecture, caching/batching diagram, dedicated pool capacity model, fallback routing flow, KV cache preservation during rollouts.
- One-page TCO model (spreadsheet link) pre-filled with example workloads.
- Short demo script: show Console live latency/cost breakdown, simulate a model fallback event, and demonstrate canary rollout steps.

Call to action and ownership

- Ask for: target workload metrics (qps distribution, P95 latency targets, typical prompt length), security checklist, and expected pilot success metrics.
- Field owner: Marcus Li (solution engineering) — contact via internal Slack #se-redeploy or email marcus.li@redwood.com.

Appendix: quick command examples (for engineers)

1) Example curl for a hosted inference call:
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
  -d '{"model":"open-llama-7b", "input":"Summarize sales brief","max_tokens":128}'

2) Canary rollout checklist (short):
  1. Create canary model variant with 5% traffic rule.
  2. Validate metric convergence for 24–48h.
  3. Monitor Console alerts for error-rate regressions.
  4. Gradually increase to 25%, 50%, then 100% with rollback guardrails.

Notes and references

- Use the TCO worksheet and the dedicated capacity spec sheet during commercial conversations.
- For deeper technical deep dives, see: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture and /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity.

Document maintenance

Owner: go-to-market field enablement. Update cadence: quarterly or after significant product/packaging changes.
